speakers.name: David Chiaverini
speakers.firm: Jefferies (operator introduced as RBC Capital Markets)

exchanges.question: How will deposit competition and betas evolve as AI smart cash tools (like JPM's) spread? Second: will JPM pursue RWA mitigation under the Basel III proposal, and how much SCB relief could removal of markets/operational risk double counting provide?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: early stages; aim is to make money management easier; may squeeze some margin, 'That's life'; JPM looks at the whole basket (ATMs, branches, advice, Zelle). Barnum: deposit competition always intense; the tool is not even live, targets a very small subset of clients with investments; an experiment. Basel: not a story about optimization; targeted RWA clarifications needed (high-yield repo collateral, advised lines); G-SIB is a significant disincentive to some markets businesses. Double count: JPM currently below the stress floor so relief depends on method; supported but not top priority. Dimon: Global Market Shock and operational risk capital are out of whack with reality; JPM already has $80 billion or $90 billion of trading book capital.

exchanges.question: Why was NII ex-Markets held at $95 billion despite asset sensitivity and fewer rate cuts? Second: if a recession brings private credit defaults, would losses to banks be systemic?
exchanges.answer: Barnum: disclosed EAR is $1.8 billion; removed cuts were back-dated so full-year average impact only ~20 basis points; small implied upward revision offset by other noise and rounding. Dimon: not systemic; private credit leveraged lending ~$1.7 trillion vs high yield ~$1.7 trillion, bank syndicated leveraged loans ~$1.7 trillion, investment grade $13 trillion, mortgage ~$13 trillion. Some weakening in underwriting; losses in a credit cycle will be worse than expected relative to the scenario; banks need very large private credit losses before being hit; excess debt is mainly government; an unexpected industry always surprises (maybe software).

exchanges.question: How did scenario weighting and macro risks factor into reserve setting this quarter? Second: drivers of strong balance sheet growth and outlook for loan and deposit growth this year.
exchanges.answer: Did not change scenario weights; economic outlook lowered weighted average unemployment in the allowance from 5.8% to 5.6%, a tailwind mainly in consumer; home lending release ~$150 million (maybe $110 million) on HPI revision; wholesale builds on loan growth and idiosyncratic downgrades. Debated adding downside skew; concluded existing conservative bias sufficient. Balance sheet growth primarily Markets, low-density secured financing, largely seasonal. Card loan growth expectation 6% or a little more unchanged; rest modest; Home Lending headwind from First Republic roll-off; Markets/data center lending opportunistic.

exchanges.question: How resilient are consumer spend and credit if energy prices stay high; any cracks? Second: any bad volatility in trading, and what drove the large rise in trading assets (business as usual or excess capital deployment)?
exchanges.answer: Nothing new: early roll rates, delinquencies, cash buffers and spend consistent with prior trends and healthy; gas/energy ~3% of typical consumer expenditure in the portfolio; no visible discretionary trade-down yet; labor market is the key, and bad Middle East outcomes hitting labor would show through. Dimon: helped by higher tax refunds. No broad bad volatility this quarter. Trading asset growth mostly BAU, seasonal, low risk density, not capital deployment; deploying excess needs both capital and liquidity freed up.

exchanges.question: How much of the $1.7 trillion private credit market is substitution from banks versus credit banks would never originate, can banks recapture share, what about collateral conservatism, and are spreads improving? Second: is 2% consumer deposit growth the start of a return to higher growth?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: the market existed before and was partly arbitrage from discouraged bank leveraged lending; hard to say, but probably half was arbitrage banks could pick up; banks value whole relationships; spreads vary by bank, no specific trend given; always had marking rights on collateral; credit not much worse except pockets; not systemic but dispersion of outcomes, business may return to banks. Barnum: 'air pocket' a strong word; too early to call a return given tax season help; consumer deposit growth expectation low to mid-single digits unchanged; over 450,000 net new checking accounts; wholesale deposits starting well but core view significantly less robust growth than last year.

exchanges.question: With 1Q expenses elevated versus the full-year guide, how will expenses come down to hit ~$105 billion? Second: how will stablecoins and digital assets affect deposits and payments?
exchanges.answer: Discouraged annualizing quarterly expenses due to Markets seasonality; JPM does not cut to meet guidance; exceptional Markets and Banking performance might otherwise have prompted an upward revision; too early to assume offsets; if every quarter were this good they would spend more than $105 billion; '$105 is not a promise.' Stablecoin: Kinexys modernizing wholesale payments (programmable money, tokenized deposits); wholesale payments already efficient, low margin, not ripe for disruption; consumer stablecoin rewards risk becoming regulatory arbitrage on interest prohibition; supports legislative certainty with same risk, same regulation.

exchanges.question: What is the opportunity in consumer interest-bearing deposit costs given the forward curve? Second: what are typical advance rates and credit enhancement on bank lending to private credit?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: deposit margin about the same as today, give or take a couple of basis points. Barnum: yield curve flows through high-beta deposits; low-beta pricing already low within a service bundle, little room. Dimon: 'asking for too much information'; senior to the underlying loans, each structure different; see BDC disclosures; BDC statutory leverage limits around one or a bit more. Barnum: senior, well diversified, conservative advance rates, sector concentration caps, cash flow trapping; comfortable.

exchanges.question: How should investors handicap LLM-enabled cyber risk and banking system preparedness? Second: will AI drive meaningful long-term efficiency ratio gains and new business opportunities?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: cyber is the largest risk (per Chairman's letter); JPM well protected, spends heavily, in constant contact with government; AI made it worse and harder; testing Mythos, which creates additional vulnerabilities; banks in total rather well protected but not everything they rely on; hygiene matters. Barnum: generative AI risks/opportunities known before latest Anthropic models headlines; on a continuum. Dimon: bad idea to expect AI to improve the efficiency ratio since competition passes benefits to the market; but it creates opportunities (Connected Commerce, fraud and scam reduction, prospecting, AI services, adjacencies).

exchanges.question: Why has trading been consistently strong across varied environments? Second: updated thoughts on capital allocation given the large excess buffer and buybacks.
exchanges.answer: Dimon: excellent people; JPM buys and sells almost $4 trillion a day; more volume and volatility widens spreads; serving investors with $350 trillion; occasional wrong-side losses are a cost of business. Barnum: deploying much more capital in markets with returns below the 17% company level but good. Dimon: excess capital around $40 billion, subject to rules; prefers deploying via client growth (bankers, overseas commercial banking, branches), large client and infrastructure needs; not in a rush; preferred use is not buying back stock today, rather buy at a real discount; wants to remove 'cash returned to investors' metric.

exchanges.question: Can public banks finance long-duration capital needs versus private markets, and how will higher-for-longer rates affect BB/B refinancing? Second: size JPM's private credit exposure.
exchanges.answer: Barnum: from $330 billion NBFI in the call report to $160 billion core NBFI; about $50 billion of that is private credit (leverage loan investors: back leverage, BDC lending); then said the leveraged loan/back leverage exposure is about $60 billion. Dimon: banks won't warehouse long-dated assets; private and public markets converging for large IG; JPM intermediates for pensions and others, keeping shorter-dated assets on balance sheet. Must be prepared for recession and stagflation; higher-for-longer with gapping spreads would stress leveraged refinancings; credit cycle worse than expected but not systemic.

exchanges.question: Has investment banking activity paused or pipeline been pushed out? Second: does the G-SIB surcharge impinge on JPM's ability to grow the markets balance sheet?
exchanges.answer: Activity held up; part of the result was accelerated M&A closings from faster-than-expected regulatory approvals; pipeline resilient, maybe surprisingly so; if Middle East situation derails, expect some impact on sentiment. G-SIB: short answer yes; it disproportionately hits Markets and low-risk-density client activity; JPM will find ways to reduce the G-SIB charge (arbitrage) while serving clients, though not great for the system.

exchanges.question: How does JPM ensure it selects top-tier private credit projects and avoids bad ones?
exchanges.answer: Disciplined on credit; turns down deals over covenants, underwriting or ability to move assets out of the secured company; willing to let the balance sheet shrink if credit gets stretched; underwrites company, loans and covenants. Would be completely fine if the loan book dropped 10% next year if loans walked away from were irresponsible.
